lead: Frequency division multiplexing (FDM) places each message in its own frequency slot and adds all slots to one cable, wire or radio band. A different carrier shifts each baseband signal into its slot. At the far end, a band-pass filter picks one slot and a demodulator brings that message back to baseband. FDM exists because one medium, such as a coaxial cable or a microwave link, can carry many telephone calls at once. Telephone trunk routes, cable television and satellite links use it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for SSB, Chapter 2.7 for receiver frequency translation, and Unit 1 for spectra.

blocks.text: One telephone voice signal occupies about 0.3 kHz to 3.4 kHz, a width of 3.1 kHz. In FDM, this baseband signal is not sent at 0 Hz. A carrier multiplies it, and an SSB filter keeps one sideband. The sideband is placed inside a reserved frequency slot. A slot is the total frequency range given to one channel. The message does not fill the whole slot. The empty strip at the edge is the guard band. For example, a 3.1 kHz voice signal in a 4 kHz slot leaves 0.9 kHz as guard band.

blocks.where: B<sub>slot</sub> is the slot width in kHz; B<sub>m</sub> is the message bandwidth in kHz; B<sub>g</sub> is the guard band in kHz.

blocks.text: For N channels, the composite bandwidth is N times the slot width. The total is not N times the voice bandwidth, because every channel also needs guard band.

blocks.where: B<sub>FDM</sub> is the total composite bandwidth in kHz; N is the number of channels; B<sub>slot</sub> is one slot width in kHz; B<sub>m</sub> is message bandwidth; B<sub>g</sub> is guard band.

blocks.text: If DSB is used instead of SSB, the sideband pair needs 2B<sub>m</sub>, so the slot becomes 2B<sub>m</sub> plus guard band. Voice FDM normally uses SSB because it halves the spectrum per call. Slots must not overlap. Overlap lets one message enter another channel, which is crosstalk.

The transmitter works channel by channel. First, a low-pass filter limits each message to 3.1 kHz. Second, each message multiplies a different carrier: f<sub>c1</sub>, f<sub>c2</sub>, and so on. Third, an SSB filter keeps one sideband. Fourth, a band-pass filter trims the result to its assigned slot. A linear summer then adds all slot signals to form the composite FDM signal.

items: Limit each message to B<sub>m</sub> with a low-pass filter.
Multiply message i by carrier f<sub>ci</sub> and keep one SSB sideband.
Band-pass filter channel i to its slot from f<sub>i</sub> to f<sub>i</sub> + B<sub>slot</sub>.
Add all filtered slot signals in a linear summer.
Send the composite signal on the cable, link or radio carrier.

blocks.text: The receiver reverses the process. A band-pass filter selects one slot and rejects the others. In a superheterodyne receiver, a mixer then translates that slot to a fixed intermediate frequency for easy filtering. An SSB demodulator multiplies by a local carrier and a low-pass filter recovers the voice. Crystal, ceramic and SAW filters are common because they have sharp edges near a slot boundary.

Filters are never perfect. A real band-pass filter has finite stop-band attenuation, so a small part of channel 1 can leak into channel 2. The guard band lowers this leakage but cannot remove it. Carrier drift also moves a slot and causes overlap. A nonlinear summer or amplifier is another danger: it creates intermodulation products that can fall inside other slots. Keep the summing and amplification linear, and leave enough guard band.

Telephone systems were the first large FDM users. A basic group carries 12 voice channels in 4 kHz slots from 60 kHz to 108 kHz. That is 12 × 4 = 48 kHz of composite band. Five groups can form a supergroup, and larger hierarchies continue from there. The same idea appears in cable television, where many TV channels share one coaxial cable, and in satellite transponders, where each uplink carrier gets a frequency slot.

When each user or terminal keeps a permanent frequency slot, some syllabi call the scheme frequency division multiple access, or FDMA. FM stereo puts the L+R sum at baseband, a 19 kHz pilot, and the L-R difference around a 38 kHz subcarrier inside one FM band; Unit 3 covers that receiver. FDM separates channels by frequency. Time division multiplexing separates channels by time and belongs to Unit 4. OFDM overlaps subcarriers so they stay orthogonal, and Unit 6 covers it.

figure.caption: Four 3.1 kHz voice channels are shifted into 4 kHz slots from 60 kHz to 76 kHz and added by a summer; the unused part of each slot is the guard band.

spec.title: Four-channel FDM
spec.aria: Four SSB channels at 60-64, 64-68, 68-72 and 72-76 kHz are added by a summer to form one composite FDM signal.

examples.question: Four voice channels, each 3.1 kHz wide, use FDM with 4 kHz slots starting at 60 kHz. Find each channel's signal band, the guard band, and the total composite bandwidth.
steps: Given: number of channels N = 4; message bandwidth B_m = 3.1 kHz; slot width B_slot = 4 kHz; first slot starts at 60 kHz.
Channel 1 slot: 60 kHz to 60 + 4 = 64 kHz. Its 3.1 kHz signal occupies 60.0 kHz to 60.0 + 3.1 = 63.1 kHz. Guard band: 63.1 kHz to 64.0 kHz, width 64.0 - 63.1 = 0.9 kHz.
Channel 2 slot: 64 kHz to 68 kHz. Signal band: 64.0 kHz to 67.1 kHz. Guard band: 67.1 kHz to 68.0 kHz, width 0.9 kHz.
Channel 3 slot: 68 kHz to 72 kHz. Signal band: 68.0 kHz to 71.1 kHz. Guard band: 71.1 kHz to 72.0 kHz, width 0.9 kHz.
Channel 4 slot: 72 kHz to 76 kHz. Signal band: 72.0 kHz to 75.1 kHz. Guard band: 75.1 kHz to 76.0 kHz, width 0.9 kHz.
Total composite bandwidth = N × B_slot = 4 × 4 = 16 kHz. Equivalently, 76 kHz - 60 kHz = 16 kHz.
examples.answer: Each slot is 4 kHz wide, the guard band is 0.9 kHz, and the composite FDM bandwidth is 16 kHz from 60 kHz to 76 kHz.
examples.check:
slot = 4.0
voice = 3.1
channels = 4
guard = slot - voice
total = channels * slot
print(round(guard, 1))
print(round(total, 1))

traps: The guard band is not message bandwidth. Total FDM bandwidth is N times slot width, not N times voice bandwidth.
Using DSB instead of SSB needs 2B<sub>m</sub> for the sidebands, so the slot becomes 2B<sub>m</sub> + B<sub>g</sub>. The slot is wider, but not exactly double.
Real filters leak. A guard band reduces crosstalk but does not remove it; finite stop-band attenuation and carrier drift still cause overlap.
A nonlinear summer or amplifier creates intermodulation products that can land in other slots. Keep the combining linear.
FDM separates channels by frequency; TDM separates channels by time. Do not use the names interchangeably.

quiz.q: Define frequency division multiplexing in one sentence.
quiz.a: FDM places each message in a separate frequency slot and adds all slots to form one composite signal.

quiz.q: What is a guard band in FDM?
quiz.a: A guard band is the unused frequency strip between adjacent message bands in neighbouring slots, kept to reduce crosstalk from imperfect filters.

quiz.q: Why is SSB preferred over DSB for voice FDM?
quiz.a: SSB needs only B<sub>m</sub> for the sideband, while DSB needs 2B<sub>m</sub>. With guard band B<sub>g</sub>, the slots are B<sub>m</sub> + B<sub>g</sub> and 2B<sub>m</sub> + B<sub>g</sub>, so SSB uses a much narrower slot but not exactly half.

quiz.q: Three voice channels, each 3.1 kHz wide, use 4 kHz slots starting at 100 kHz. Find the guard band, the three slot ranges, and the total composite bandwidth.
quiz.a: Guard band = 4 - 3.1 = 0.9 kHz. Slots: 100-104 kHz, 104-108 kHz, 108-112 kHz. Total bandwidth = 3 × 4 = 12 kHz.

quiz.q: A basic telephone group has 12 channels in 4 kHz slots from 60 kHz to 108 kHz. Verify its total bandwidth and state the guard band per channel for 3.1 kHz voice.
quiz.a: Total bandwidth = 108 - 60 = 48 kHz = 12 × 4 kHz. Guard band = 4 - 3.1 = 0.9 kHz per channel.

quiz.q: Channel 2 in an FDM link suffers crosstalk from channel 1. Give two likely causes and one practical fix.
quiz.a: Causes: channel 1 band-pass filter has insufficient stop-band attenuation, or carrier drift moved channel 1 toward channel 2, or the summer/amplifier is nonlinear. Fix: increase guard band, use sharper filters such as SAW or crystal filters, and stabilise carriers.

quiz.q: Why must the summer in an FDM transmitter be linear?
quiz.a: A linear summer adds the slot signals without creating new frequencies. A nonlinear summer mixes slots and produces intermodulation products that can fall inside other slots; those products appear as crosstalk and cannot be removed by the receiver band-pass filter.

beyond: Not for the exam. FDM ideas appear in DSL, cable television, satellite transponders and analog radio links. Modern systems often use OFDM, which overlaps subcarriers so they remain orthogonal without wide guard bands. Search for frequency division multiple access, telephone group and supergroup hierarchies, and orthogonal frequency division multiplexing.
